fixes.explanation: Afraid does show up in this passage, but it's in a different spot. Paul tells the Gentiles, “Do not be arrogant, but be afraid.” (Romans 11:20). Here in verse 11, the word aimed at Israel is jealous. Same letter, different verse, and I've been known to grab the oven mitt when I wanted the spatula.

Not this verse, friend. Paul hopes to provoke his own people to jealousy “…and save some of them.” He doesn't say judge. He says save, and that tells you where his heart is pointed: toward rescuing them, not sentencing them.

It's a pretty phrase, but it's not what Paul says here. He asks, “…what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?” Life from the dead is his answer. Light to the nations is a nice thought, but it isn't what this verse says.

Grief isn't what he says here. Paul tells the shoot, “…do not boast over those branches.” Paul himself writes of great sorrow for his own people, Israel (Romans 9:2–3), but that's a different spot in the letter. In this verse the warning is about boasting.

It's true, and Paul says it plainly. His words are, “You do not support the root, but the root supports you.” So the grafted-in shoot isn't the one supporting the root. The root is supporting the shoot. I'd say that's good news for any branch.

Works is a common guess, but it's not what Paul says. He says, “…but you stand by faith.” Faith is the word that goes in the blank. Unbelief is why the natural branches were broken off, and faith is how the shoot stands.

Those sound like good things to say about God, but they're not the two Paul names here. He says to take notice of “…the kindness and severity of God…” Paul does speak of God's wisdom a few verses later (Romans 11:33). In verse 22, the two things are kindness and severity.

Those aren't the two Paul names in this verse. He says, “Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God…” That's his pair. Severity goes to those who fell, and kindness goes to the grafted-in Gentiles who continue in it.

It's actually true. Paul says, “And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.” So for those branches, grafting back in is on the table. That's good news, and I'd hold onto it.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, “…how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!” Readily means more easily, not less. If a wild shoot can be grafted in, the natural ones fit their own tree even better.
